notes:
Task and constraints: Count four-directionally connected groups of '1' cells in a nonempty binary grid.
Idea: Scan every cell and launch an iterative depth-first search whenever an unvisited land cell is found.
Technique and why it applies: The nested dfs uses a stack and marks each discovered land cell as water before pushing it. This prevents it from being added repeatedly and avoids a separate visited matrix.
Invariant: Every cell changed from '1' to '0' has already been discovered as part of the current component or was already water; each successful dfs call accounts for one island.
Edge cases: All-water grids return zero; isolated land cells each add one. The code includes an unused UnionFind class whose self.set starts as range and would not support assignment, but numIslands never invokes it.
Complexity: Each grid cell is examined and each land cell pushed at most once, giving O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case stack space. The author labels are correct.

Task and constraints: Count islands made from horizontally or vertically adjacent land cells.
Idea: Sweep the grid and use breadth-first search to erase each connected land component.
Technique and why it applies: A deque stores the current frontier; each popped coordinate checks four neighbors, marks land as water immediately, and enqueues it. Marking on enqueue avoids duplicate queue entries.
Invariant: During a BFS call, the queue contains discovered cells in the current component that still need their neighbors processed; all discovered land has been changed to '0'.
Edge cases: An all-water grid returns zero and a single land cell contributes one. The UnionFind helper is unused; its range-backed set would fail if called, but it does not affect this method.
Complexity: Each cell is processed at most once, so time is O(mn); the queue can hold O(mn) cells in the worst case. No complexity labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the bitwise AND of every integer in the inclusive range [left, right], where zero is allowed.
Idea: Starting at left, jump to the next number with the lowest set bit cleared, while accumulating AND results until the next jump would exceed right.
Technique and why it applies: cur & -cur isolates the least significant set bit; adding it advances to the next number that changes the lower-bit pattern. The accumulated left &= cur retains bits common to visited values.
Invariant: left contains only bits that have survived the AND with all visited values, and cur is a visited range value.
Edge cases: left=0 returns zero immediately. The unused i variable has no effect. This method relies on the jump sequence representing the relevant bit changes throughout the range.
Complexity: The number of jumps is bounded by the integer bit width, so time is O(log right) and auxiliary space O(1). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the bitwise AND of all integers from m through n, inclusive.
Idea: Find how many right shifts are needed for the difference n-m to become zero, then clear that many low bits of the common prefix.
Technique and why it applies: Numbers in the range share the same high-order prefix; the changing lower bits cannot remain set in the AND. The shift count derived from the difference identifies the number of potentially varying bits.
Invariant: i counts the bit positions needed to reduce diff to zero; n >> i and m >> i therefore retain the common high prefix.
Edge cases: When m equals n, diff is zero and i remains zero, so the expression returns that number. Operator precedence makes the final expression equivalent to n & ((m >> i) << i).
Complexity: The loop takes O(log(n-m+1)) time and O(1) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the common bitwise-AND result for every integer in [m,n].
Idea: Repeatedly clear the least significant set bit of n until n is no longer greater than m.
Technique and why it applies: n &= n-1 removes one set bit. If n remains above m, that bit cannot survive the AND of every number in the interval; continuing eventually leaves the common prefix.
Invariant: The current n is the result of clearing set bits that cannot be present in the range-wide AND.
Edge cases: If m=n, the loop is skipped and the number is returned unchanged. If the interval crosses a power-of-two boundary, clearing continues until only the common high prefix remains.
Complexity: The loop executes at most the number of set bits in n, bounded by O(log n), rather than O(1) for arbitrary integer width. Auxiliary space is O(1). The author’s O(1) time label is inaccurate for general integer inputs; O(1) space is correct.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a positive integer eventually reaches 1 under repeated replacement by the sum of its squared decimal digits.
Idea: Store every number encountered and stop if the sequence reaches 1 or repeats a previous value.
Technique and why it applies: The set detects cycles: once a number repeats, the deterministic transformation will repeat the same cycle forever. The list comprehension squares each digit and sums the results.
Invariant: hset contains all prior sequence values, so membership proves the process has entered a cycle that does not terminate at 1.
Edge cases: n=1 returns True without entering the loop. A cycle such as the one reached from 2 returns False. The input is positive, as required by the statement.
Complexity: If k distinct sequence values are visited and d is the maximum digit count, time is O(kd) and the set uses O(k) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return whether the positive integer is happy according to the repeated sum-of-squared-digits process.
Idea: Continue transforming n while it is not 1 and has not appeared in a lookup dictionary.
Technique and why it applies: The dictionary records visited values; repetition proves the deterministic sequence has entered a cycle. nextNumber processes the decimal representation and accumulates each digit's square.
Invariant: lookup contains every value already transformed, so the loop exits only at 1 or on revisiting a value.
Edge cases: Starting at 1 returns True immediately. A repeated non-1 value returns False. The author supplies space complexity O(k), where k is the number of visited values.
Complexity: Each transformation costs O(d) for d digits, so total time is O(kd), often summarized as O(k) when digit work is bounded; dictionary storage is O(k). The stated space label is consistent.

Task and constraints: Count primes strictly below n, with n as large as five million.
Idea: Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes: begin by treating values as prime, then mark multiples of each prime as composite.
Technique and why it applies: The loop processes candidate divisors while i*i<n; marking starts at i*i because smaller multiples have already been handled by smaller factors. The final count returns the remaining True entries.
Invariant: Before processing i, all composite numbers with a smaller prime factor have been marked; truth[i] therefore identifies whether i is still prime.
Edge cases: n<2 returns zero before indexing truth[0] and truth[1]. The list is allocated before this check, which is safe for n=0 or 1.
Complexity: Sieve marking takes O(n log log n) time, and the boolean list uses O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count prime numbers less than n; this version uses a linear sieve and returns the number of generated primes below n.
Idea: Maintain the smallest prime factor for each integer and build a list of primes as the scan advances.
Technique and why it applies: A number with no recorded smallest factor is prime. Each known prime marks i*p, while the conditions stop products beyond n or when p exceeds i's smallest prime factor, limiting duplicate composite work.
Invariant: spf[x] records the smallest prime factor for each composite x reached so far; every prime up to the limit is appended once.
Edge cases: Calling the helper with n-1 handles the strict “less than n” requirement. For n=0 or 1, the helper receives a nonpositive limit and returns an empty list because its range loops do not execute.
Complexity: The linear sieve is O(n) time and O(n) space, matching the author labels. Despite the filename suffix TLE, the shown algorithm is a linear sieve.

Task and constraints: Count primes strictly less than n, using a compact sieve that stores candidates for odd integers only.
Idea: Start with a True flag for each odd-index slot, then mark odd multiples of each surviving odd prime as composite.
Technique and why it applies: The slot i//2 represents odd number i. Composite marking begins at i*i and advances by 2*i, skipping even multiples that are already non-prime.
Invariant: cnt starts at the number of represented odd values and is decremented once whenever a still-true composite slot is marked. The value 2 is not represented in the array.
Edge cases: n<=2 returns zero. For n>2, cnt is initialized to len(is_prime), which counts all odd slots below n, including 1; the code never marks slot 0 false. Therefore the returned count is one too high for every n>2.
Complexity: The sieve takes O(n log log n) time and O(n) space. The author’s O(n) space label is correct, but the implementation has a correctness error in its initial count.

Task and constraints: Decide whether equal-length strings are isomorphic: each source character must map consistently, and distinct source characters cannot map to the same target character.
Idea: Build a mapping from s characters to t characters, reject a target already used by another source character, then reconstruct the mapped string and compare it with t.
Technique and why it applies: The dictionary enforces a forward mapping, while checking dict1.values() prevents two source characters from sharing a target. The final reconstruction verifies all positions.
Invariant: After each pair, dict1 maps every processed source character to its target character; the uniqueness check prevents a conflicting reverse assignment.
Edge cases: Repeated source characters must always map to the same target; the final reconstruction catches overwritten mappings. The code uses string concatenation in a loop, which can be costly.
Complexity: With n characters, repeated membership in dict1.values() and keys can cost O(n) per iteration, making worst-case time O(n²); building m also can be quadratic due to immutable concatenation. Space is O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Decide whether all courses can be completed given prerequisite pairs, where each pair [course, prerequisite] represents a directed dependency.
Idea: Apply Kahn-style topological processing using sets of courses with no dependents in the code's reversed edge representation.
Technique and why it applies: pre stores prerequisites for each course and dep stores dependents. Removing a processed course from its prerequisites' dependent sets exposes more courses to process; a cycle prevents all courses from entering l.
Invariant: l contains processed courses, and s contains courses whose dependent set is empty according to this representation.
Edge cases: No prerequisites lets every course be processed. A directed cycle leaves l shorter than numCourses. The comments about incoming edges are somewhat confusing, but the updates are designed around the reversed bookkeeping.
Complexity: Each course and prerequisite edge is handled a constant number of times on average, giving O(V+E) expected time and O(V+E) space for sets and the processed list. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return whether the prerequisite graph permits finishing every course.
Idea: Build adjacency lists and indegrees, then repeatedly remove a course whose indegree is zero.
Technique and why it applies: For each pair [u,v], the code records edge v→u and increments u's indegree. Processing a zero-indegree course decrements its dependents; newly zero indegrees are pushed onto the stack.
Invariant: in_degree tracks the number of prerequisites still unsatisfied for each course; result contains courses removed in a valid topological order.
Edge cases: If there are no edges, all courses start in stk and the result length matches numCourses. A cycle leaves at least one course unprocessed, returning False. Duplicate imports do not change behavior.
Complexity: Each vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times on average, giving O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether all courses can be completed from prerequisite pairs.
Idea: Use Kahn's topological algorithm, processing the graph in layers with a list of currently available courses.
Technique and why it applies: in_degree counts prerequisites, while adj maps each prerequisite to the courses unlocked by completing it. Every processed course decrements its dependents and places newly zero-indegree courses in new_q.
Invariant: At the start of each layer, q contains all courses made available by the previous layer; result contains a topological prefix.
Edge cases: An empty prerequisite list processes every course. If a cycle exists, some courses never reach indegree zero and the final length check returns False. Repeated imports are redundant.
Complexity: Building the graph and processing each vertex and edge costs O(V+E) expected time; adjacency, indegrees, queues, and result use O(V+E) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target; all array values and target are positive.
Idea: Expand a right boundary while accumulating values, then shrink the left boundary as long as the current window meets the target.
Technique and why it applies: Positive values make the window sum monotonic under expansion and contraction. Each left and right pointer only moves forward, so the nested while loop does not imply quadratic work.
Invariant: s equals the sum of nums[l:r+1] after each right-end addition and before the next expansion; ans stores the shortest qualifying window found so far.
Edge cases: If no window qualifies, ans remains len(nums)+1 and the method returns zero. A single value at least target yields length one.
Complexity: Each element enters and leaves the window at most once, so time is O(n), with O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return a valid order for all courses, or an empty list if prerequisites contain a cycle.
Idea: Build a prerequisite adjacency list and run depth-first search with separate sets for active recursion and completed courses.
Technique and why it applies: A course in cycle is on the current recursion path, so encountering it detects a cycle. visit memoizes fully explored courses; appending after exploring prerequisites creates reverse dependency order.
Invariant: cycle tracks the active DFS path, while visit contains courses already proven acyclic; output stores each completed course after its prerequisites.
Edge cases: A cycle immediately returns an empty list. With no edges, each course is appended. The returned output is already prerequisite-first because prerequisites are appended before the course.
Complexity: Each course and edge is visited at most once, so O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space. Recursive depth can reach V and may hit Python's recursion limit for sufficiently deep graphs. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Produce a topological order of all courses, or return an empty list if a cycle prevents completion.
Idea: Construct adjacency and indegree structures, then process zero-indegree courses with a stack.
Technique and why it applies: Each prerequisite pair creates an edge from prerequisite v to course u. Removing a course decreases indegrees of its outgoing neighbors, which become available at zero.
Invariant: result is always a valid topological prefix; in_degree records remaining incoming prerequisites for each course.
Edge cases: No edges returns all courses in some order. If a cycle exists, the stack empties before all courses are processed and the method returns an empty list. Repeated imports are harmless.
Complexity: Graph construction and traversal take O(V+E) expected time; adjacency, indegree map, stack, and output require O(V+E) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find a course ordering that respects every prerequisite, or return an empty list when a cycle exists.
Idea: Run DFS with three colors: WHITE means unseen, GRAY means active, and BLACK means completely explored.
Technique and why it applies: A GRAY node indicates a back edge to the current recursion path and signals a cycle; BLACK nodes can be reused without re-exploration. Courses are appended after their prerequisite neighbors.
Invariant: lookup[u] is GRAY during active exploration and BLACK after successful completion; result is a postorder traversal.
Edge cases: Encountering GRAY returns False and causes the top-level method to return an empty list. With no prerequisites, each course is appended once. The code builds adj[u] with prerequisites, so postorder appending places prerequisites before the course.
Complexity: Each vertex and edge is processed at most once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space, including recursion and adjacency. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return any valid topological ordering of the course graph, or an empty list if a cycle exists.
Idea: DFS from every course, using WHITE/GRAY/BLACK states to detect active-path cycles and avoid revisiting completed nodes.
Technique and why it applies: The adjacency list stores edges from prerequisite v to dependent course u. Postorder appends a course after exploring its outgoing dependents, so reversing the result places prerequisites before dependents.
Invariant: GRAY nodes are active and detect cycles; BLACK nodes are complete. result contains completed nodes in postorder until all reachable nodes are explored.
Edge cases: A cycle causes dfs to return False and the method returns an empty list. An isolated course is appended and included. The repeated collections imports are redundant.
Complexity: The DFS processes each vertex and edge once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space for graph, color map, result, and recursion. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find an ordering of all courses satisfying prerequisite edges, returning an empty list if not all courses can be ordered.
Idea: Use Kahn's algorithm with a queue-like list processed in layers.
Technique and why it applies: The code records each prerequisite-to-course edge and increments the dependent course's indegree. Each layer is processed into a new_q of courses whose indegree just became zero.
Invariant: result is a valid topological prefix; q contains the currently available courses, and in_degree counts prerequisites not yet processed.
Edge cases: With no prerequisites, the first layer contains every course. A cycle leaves some courses unprocessed, so the final length test returns an empty list. Repeated imports are redundant.
Complexity: Each vertex and edge is handled a constant number of times on average, giving O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space. No labels were supplied.
